nameStory: The Irregular Earth Tongue gets its name from its tongue-like shape that emerges from the forest floor, looking like a yellow-orange tongue poking up through the leaf litter. The "irregular" part refers to its somewhat wavy, bumpy surface that's never perfectly smooth like you might expect a tongue to be.
description: This unusual fungus looks like a small, bright yellow to orange tongue or club sticking up from the ground. It's quite small, typically only 1-3 inches tall and about as wide as your pinky finger. Unlike mushrooms with caps and stems, earth tongues are simple, club-shaped fruiting bodies that can be slightly flattened or rounded. The bright color makes them stand out against the dark forest floor.

idTips.label: Bright yellow-orange color
idTips.description: Vivid yellow to orange coloration that's hard to miss against dark soil and leaves, like a tiny traffic cone in the woods

idTips.label: Club or tongue shape
idTips.description: Simple, elongated club shape that's often slightly flattened, feeling firm but slightly spongy when gently pressed

idTips.label: Irregular surface
idTips.description: Surface has subtle bumps and waves rather than being perfectly smooth, with a slightly waxy feel

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically 1-3 inches tall and pencil-thin, easy to overlook unless you're looking carefully

idTips.label: Grows from soil
idTips.description: Emerges directly from rich, organic soil or leaf litter, often partially buried at the base

habitat: Found in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under hardwood trees like maples and oaks. Prefers areas with deep leaf litter and well-decomposed organic matter in the soil. Often grows in small scattered groups rather than large clusters.

seasonality.spring: Not typically visible in spring, as fruiting bodies haven't developed yet.
seasonality.summer: Fruiting bodies begin to appear in mid to late summer, starting small and gradually developing their full size.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding mature specimens, when the bright colors are most vibrant and specimens reach full size.
seasonality.winter: May persist into early winter in mild years, but fruiting bodies eventually shrivel and disappear.

funFact: Despite looking like a simple fungus, the Irregular Earth Tongue is actually one of the most evolutionarily distinct fungi in North America - it's so unique that it sits in its own order, separate from all other fungi, like being the only member of an exclusive club that diverged from other fungi millions of years ago!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small club fungi, but the bright yellow-orange color is distinctive - most other small clubs are brown, black, or pale colored. Remember: if it's tongue-shaped and traffic-cone colored, you've likely found an earth tongue.
contextualKnowledge: The name "earth tongue" is used for several different groups of fungi that aren't closely related, which can be confusing. True earth tongues (like Geoglossum) are typically dark-colored, while Neolecta species are the bright yellow-orange ones that also get called earth tongues.
compareHints: The only close relative in New England is the Golden Earth Tongue (Neolecta vitellina), which is more consistently golden-yellow rather than orange, and tends to be smoother and more regularly shaped. The Irregular Earth Tongue typically shows more surface texture and color variation from yellow to orange.
